items.prompt: A 2-input AND gate outputs 1 under which condition?

options.label: The two inputs are different
Both inputs are 1
At least one input is 1
Both inputs are 0

rubric: AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1.
Choosing 'at least one' confuses AND with OR.

items.prompt: Which 2-input gate outputs 1 only when its inputs are different?

options.label: NAND
XOR
NOR
XNOR

rubric: XOR is 1 when the inputs differ.
XNOR is the opposite (1 when equal); learners often swap them.

items.prompt: In Boolean algebra, what does `A + A'` simplify to?

options.label: A
A'

rubric: A variable ORed with its complement is always 1 (complement law).
Answer 0 mixes it up with `A · A'`.

items.prompt: Which flip-flop copies its single data input to Q on the active clock edge, so that Q equals the previous input value after each edge?

options.label: SR flip-flop
D flip-flop
T flip-flop
JK flip-flop

rubric: The D flip-flop stores its D input at the clock edge.
T, SR and JK have different input sets and behaviours.

items.prompt: What is the minimum number of flip-flops needed for a binary counter with 16 distinct states?
rubric: n flip-flops give 2^n states, so 16 states need 4.
Answering 16 confuses the number of states with the number of flip-flops.

items.prompt: Which of the following gates are universal gates, meaning any Boolean function can be built from that gate alone? Select all that apply.

options.label: NOR
NAND
XOR
AND
NOT

rubric: NAND and NOR can each build AND, OR and NOT.
AND, XOR and NOT alone cannot implement every function.

items.prompt: You are labelling a half adder diagram. It has two 1-bit inputs, A and B, and two outputs, Sum and Carry. You must name the single gate that produces the Sum output.

options.label: AND
XOR
OR
XNOR

rubric: Sum of two bits is 1 only when they differ, which is XOR.
AND produces the Carry output, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: According to De Morgan's theorem, which expression equals `(A · B)'`?

options.label: A · B'
A + B
A' · B'
A' + B'

rubric: Complementing an AND gives the OR of the complements.
A' · B' is the equivalent for a complemented OR, a frequent confusion.

items.prompt: Why is a flip-flop classed as sequential logic rather than combinational logic?

options.label: Its output changes after a delay, unlike combinational gates
Its output depends on stored state as well as current inputs
It uses more gates than a combinational circuit does
It can only be built from NAND gates and no other gate

rubric: Sequential circuits have memory, so output depends on past history too.
All gates have propagation delay, so delay does not distinguish them.

items.prompt: How many select lines does a 4-to-1 multiplexer need to choose among its data inputs?
rubric: Two select bits give 4 combinations, one per data input.
Answering 4 equates select lines with data inputs.

items.prompt: A full adder receives A = 1, B = 1 and Cin = 1. What are its outputs?

options.label: Sum = 0, Cout = 0
Sum = 1, Cout = 0
Sum = 0, Cout = 1
Sum = 1, Cout = 1

rubric: 1+1+1 = 3, which is binary 11, so Sum = 1 and Cout = 1.
Sum = 0 comes from forgetting the carry-in.

items.prompt: A T flip-flop has T = 1 held constant. What does its output Q do on each active clock edge?

options.label: It holds its previous value until T changes
It toggles to the opposite value
It is reset to 0 and stays there until T changes
It is set to 1 and stays there until T changes

rubric: With T = 1 the flip-flop toggles each clock edge, which makes it a divide-by-2.
Holding applies when T = 0.

items.prompt: Which of the following circuits are purely combinational, with outputs determined only by current inputs? Select all that apply.

options.label: 3-bit binary counter
Full adder
4-to-1 multiplexer
2-to-4 decoder
Shift register

rubric: Adders, multiplexers and decoders have no memory elements.
Counters and shift registers store state in flip-flops.

items.prompt: A 3-bit binary ripple counter is clocked by an 8 kHz square wave. Q0 is the least significant bit and Q2 the most significant. You connect an oscilloscope to Q2 and want to predict its frequency.

options.label: 1 kHz
2 kHz
8 kHz
4 kHz

rubric: Each stage divides by 2, so Q2 is 8 kHz / 8 = 1 kHz.
4 kHz is the Q0 frequency; learners forget that each stage halves again.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the output of a two-input XOR gate?

options.label: It is 1 when exactly one input is 1
It is 1 when both inputs have the same value
It is 1 when at least one input is 1
It is 1 when both inputs are 1

rubric: XOR is 1 only when the inputs differ.
Choosing 'same value' describes XNOR; 'at least one' describes OR.

items.prompt: How does a sequential circuit differ from a combinational circuit?

options.label: Its output depends only on past inputs, never current ones
Its output depends on stored state as well as current inputs
Its output is analog while a combinational output is digital
Its design uses more gates but no feedback or memory

rubric: Sequential circuits contain memory, so state matters along with the inputs.
Distractors confuse the dependence on time or confuse sequential with analog.

items.prompt: A positive-edge-triggered D flip-flop has D = 1 just before a rising clock edge and D changes to 0 just after it. What is Q after the edge?

options.label: Q becomes 1 because D was 1 at the clock edge
Q follows D and becomes 0 right after the edge
Q stays undefined until the next falling edge
Q toggles to the opposite of its previous value

rubric: A D flip-flop samples D at the active edge and holds that value.
Following D continuously describes a transparent latch; toggling describes a T flip-flop.

items.prompt: Why is the NAND gate called a universal gate?

options.label: It outputs 1 only when all of its inputs are 1
It uses less power than every other type of gate
It is the only gate that can have more than two inputs
Any Boolean function can be built using only NAND gates

rubric: Universality means NOT, AND and OR can all be built from NAND alone.
The last distractor misstates the NAND truth table (that is AND).

items.prompt: In a half adder that adds two single bits A and B, which expression gives the carry output?

options.label: A OR B
A NAND B
A XOR B
A AND B

rubric: A carry occurs only when both bits are 1, which is A AND B.
A XOR B is the sum output, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: Which of the following are combinational circuits? Select all that apply.

options.label: 2-to-4 decoder
4-to-1 multiplexer
4-bit binary counter
D flip-flop

items.prompt: A door controller opens the door when a button is pressed. The door must stay open after the button is released, until a close sensor triggers. A student asks whether the controller is combinational or sequential. Which answer is correct?

options.label: Sequential, because it has more than one input signal and so must monitor both over time
Combinational, because the button and the sensor are its only inputs and the door is its only output
Combinational, because its behaviour can be drawn using only AND and OR gates with feedback
Sequential, because the output must remember that the button was pressed earlier

rubric: Holding the door open after the input vanishes requires stored state.
Counting inputs or gate types does not decide whether a circuit is sequential.

items.prompt: Simplify the expression `A·B + A·B'` using Boolean algebra.

options.label: B
A + B
A

rubric: Factor out A: A(B + B') = A·1 = A.
Choosing B or A + B comes from misapplying the complement law.

items.prompt: For `F = A·B + C` with three inputs A, B, C, in how many of the 8 input combinations is F equal to 1?
rubric: C = 1 gives 4 combinations; with C = 0, only A = B = 1 adds one more, total 5.
Answering 4 ignores the A·B term; 6 double counts.

items.prompt: A 3-bit binary up counter currently holds 101. What value does it hold after two more clock pulses?
rubric: 101 goes to 110 and then to 111.
110 is the value after one pulse only.

items.prompt: A full adder receives A = 1, B = 1 and Cin = 1. What are its outputs?

options.label: Sum 0, Carry 0
Sum 0, Carry 1
Sum 1, Carry 0
Sum 1, Carry 1

rubric: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, which is binary 11: sum 1, carry 1.
Sum 0, carry 1 comes from forgetting the carry input.

items.prompt: A 4-bit shift register shifts right on each clock pulse, with serial input fixed at 0. It holds 1011. What does it hold after two clock pulses?
rubric: One right shift gives 0101; a second gives 0010.
0101 is the result after only one pulse; 1100 is a left shift.

items.prompt: Which of the following expressions are equal to A for all values of A and B? Select all that apply.

options.label: A·(A + B)
A·B + A·B'
A + A·B
A + A'·B

rubric: Absorption gives A + AB = A and A(A + B) = A; factoring gives AB + AB' = A.
A + A'B simplifies to A + B, not A.

items.prompt: A design uses an 8 kHz clock to drive a 2-bit binary up counter built from flip-flops. The counter's most significant bit output is connected to a slow indicator. You need to know the frequency of that output signal. What is it?

options.label: 1 kHz
4 kHz
8 kHz
2 kHz

rubric: Each counter bit halves the frequency: LSB is 4 kHz, MSB is 2 kHz.
4 kHz is the least significant bit's frequency.

items.prompt: Simplify F = A'B + AB + A'B' using Boolean algebra.

options.label: A + B'
A'B
A' + B
A + B

rubric: A'B + AB = B, and B + A'B' = A' + B by absorption of the complement.
A + B' is the complement of the result, a common slip when reading the truth table.

items.prompt: A 4:1 multiplexer has select lines S1 = A and S0 = B. To implement F = A XOR B, which values must be wired to data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 (in that order)?
rubric: XOR is 1 only when AB = 01 or 10, which select I1 and I2.
1, 0, 0, 1 implements XNOR, and 0, 1, 1, 1 implements OR.

items.prompt: A 4-bit ripple-carry adder adds A = 0110 and B = 0111 with carry-in 0. What are the sum bits and the final carry-out?

options.label: Sum 1101, carry-out 1
Sum 1101, carry-out 0
Sum 0001, carry-out 1
Sum 1100, carry-out 0

rubric: 6 + 7 = 13 = 1101, which fits in 4 bits so no carry-out occurs.
Sum 0001 with carry 1 would be the result of an overflow such as 15 + 2.

items.prompt: A 3-bit serial-in shift register is cleared to Q2Q1Q0 = 000. Serial data enters Q2 and shifts toward Q0 on each rising clock edge. The input is 1, then 1, then 0 on three successive edges. What is Q2Q1Q0 afterwards?
rubric: After three shifts the newest bit (0) is in Q2 and the earliest bits (1, 1) have moved to Q1 and Q0.
110 reverses the shift direction.

items.prompt: A 4-bit synchronous binary up-counter has a synchronous clear that forces 0000 at the next clock edge whenever the count equals 1100 (decimal 12). How many distinct states does it cycle through?

options.label: 11, counting 0 through 10
13, counting 0 through 12
16, counting 0 through 15
12, counting 0 through 11

rubric: A synchronous clear acts on the next edge, so state 12 is held for a full clock period before returning to 0.
12 states would result from decoding 1011, or from an asynchronous clear on 1100, which only glitches through 12.

items.prompt: Apply De Morgan's laws to F = (AB + C)'. Which expressions are equal to F? Select all that apply.

options.label: A'B'C'
A'B' + C'
(AB)'C'

rubric: A'B'C' and A'B' + C' come from complementing each literal without correctly swapping the operators.

items.prompt: A technician chains two JK flip-flops, both with J = K = 1 and triggered on the falling clock edge. The Q output of the first drives the clock input of the second. A 1 kHz square wave clocks the first flip-flop. What is the frequency of the second flip-flop's Q output?

options.label: 250 Hz
125 Hz
500 Hz
1 kHz

rubric: Each toggle stage divides the frequency by 2, so two stages divide by 4.
500 Hz counts only the first stage.

items.prompt: F = AB + A'C is built from two AND gates, an inverter and an OR gate. With B = 1 and C = 1, A falls from 1 to 0 and the output briefly dips to 0. What is the cause and the standard fix?

options.label: Excess fan-out on input A; replace the inverter with a NAND
Unequal delays on the A and A' paths; add the redundant term BC
Race between inputs B and C; place a flip-flop on each input
Setup violation at the OR gate; reduce the clock frequency

rubric: This is a static-1 hazard: one product term turns off before the other turns on, and the consensus term BC covers the gap.
The circuit is purely combinational, so clock-related fixes do not apply.

items.prompt: A NOR-based SR latch has S = R = 1, forcing both outputs to 0. Then S and R both return to 0 at almost the same moment. Why is the resulting state a problem?

options.label: It toggles once, because both gates then see a 0 on the other input
It is unpredictable, because the faster gate wins the race and may oscillate
It holds the earlier value, because the latch keeps its previous state
It goes to Q = 1, because the set input has priority over reset

rubric: Both gates see 0 inputs simultaneously and race to switch, so the final state depends on gate delays and may be metastable.
Latches have no built-in priority between S and R, and the previous value was lost when both outputs were forced to 0.

items.prompt: On a 3-variable K-map for F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,3,7), a student circles minterms 0 and 3 as a pair, claiming it eliminates one variable. Which statement identifies the flaw?

options.label: Minterm 0 can only be grouped using the wraparound edge of the map
Groups of two are invalid when the function has three minterms
A pair must include the minterm with the highest index to be valid
Minterms 000 and 011 differ in two bits, so they are not adjacent

rubric: Only cells that differ in exactly one variable can merge to eliminate that variable.
The other options invent grouping rules that do not exist in K-map simplification.

items.prompt: A design has two register-to-register paths with logic delays of 6 ns and 9 ns. Clock-to-Q is 1 ns and setup time is 1 ns for every flip-flop. The design fails at 100 MHz (10 ns period). What is the cause?

options.label: Setup violation on the 9 ns path, which needs 11 ns
Setup violation on the 9 ns path, because only the logic delay counts and 9 ns exceeds the 8 ns left after setup and clock-to-Q
Both paths pass, so the failure must come from clock skew
Hold violation on the 6 ns path, which is too fast

rubric: The minimum period is clk-to-Q + longest logic + setup = 1 + 9 + 1 = 11 ns, exceeding 10 ns.
The 6 ns path needs only 8 ns, and hold violations do not depend on the clock period.

items.prompt: A state machine's output sometimes changes in the middle of a clock cycle when the input changes, and the designer wants the output to change only at clock edges. Which diagnosis and remedy fit?

options.label: The state encoding is one-hot; switch to a binary encoding
The state register is asynchronous; replace it with a latch
It is a Moore machine whose outputs depend on inputs; use Mealy outputs
It is a Mealy machine whose outputs depend on inputs; use Moore outputs

rubric: Mealy outputs are functions of both state and input, so they can change whenever the input does.
Moore outputs depend only on state, so they change only after a clock edge; encoding does not alter this.

items.prompt: A 3-bit counter is designed for 5 states (0 to 4), leaving states 5 to 7 unused with don't-care next states. Which concerns are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Unused states force the design to need a fourth flip-flop
The don't-care choices may form a lockup loop among unused states
Unused states make the circuit asynchronous instead of synchronous
Power-up noise could put it in an unused state

rubric: Unused states can be entered at power-up or by a glitch, and the minimised logic may never return to a valid state.
Three flip-flops are enough for 5 states, and unused states do not change the clocking style.

items.prompt: A designer builds a full adder with Sum = A xor B xor Cin, but writes the carry as Cout = AB + Cin·A·B by mistake, using AND in place of XOR in the second term. Testing shows Sum is always right but Cout is wrong for some inputs. Which input combination exposes the fault?
rubric: The correct Cout is AB + Cin(A xor B); with A=1, B=0, Cin=1 it should be 1, but the faulty expression gives 0.
In the other three cases both expressions agree, since AB = 1 or both A and B are 0.

items.prompt: A circuit computes F = A·B + A'·C. With B = 1 and C = 1 held constant, A falls from 1 to 0 and F briefly dips to 0. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The OR gate is slower than the AND gates, so it holds F low until both products settle; a buffer after the OR would remove the dip.
The output is a static-0 hazard caused by A changing while B and C are 1; ANDing F with the term (A + A') would hold the output steady.
The expression is not minimal, so a redundant term causes the dip; removing the term A'C would eliminate the glitch.
The inverter delays A', so AB falls before A'C rises and both are briefly 0; adding the consensus term BC covers the gap.

rubric: The inverter delay lets both product terms be 0 for a moment (static-1 hazard); the consensus term BC stays 1 and covers the transition.
Distractors blame the OR gate or call it a static-0 hazard, and the last one wrongly treats redundancy as the cause when it is the cure.

items.prompt: A Moore and a Mealy sequence detector are both clocked synchronously, but their inputs may change at any time between clock edges. Why can only the Mealy output show glitches between edges?

options.label: Its output logic is clocked on both edges, so an input change just after either edge reaches the output late.
Its next-state logic is faster, so the state register changes before the input is stable and corrupts the output.
It needs fewer states, so its flip-flops are loaded more often and switching noise couples onto the output.
Its output depends combinationally on the inputs as well as the state, so mid-cycle input changes reach it.

rubric: A Mealy output is a combinational function of state and inputs, so input changes between edges propagate directly; a Moore output depends only on state registers.
Distractors invent clocking or state-count effects that do not exist in the definition.

items.prompt: A 4-bit asynchronous ripple counter (each flip-flop clocked by the previous stage's output, counting up) changes from 0111 to 1000. Ignoring the starting state, which sequence of states can be observed on Q3Q2Q1Q0 during the change, ending in the final state?
rubric: Each stage toggles only after the previous one falls, so bits clear from Q0 upward before Q3 sets: 0110, 0100, 0000, 1000.
Distractors reverse the ripple direction or let bits change in the wrong order, as if the stages shared a clock.

items.prompt: A timing report shows a hold violation between two flip-flops on the same clock; the capturing clock arrives later than the launching clock because of skew. Which statement is correct?

options.label: Lowering the clock frequency will clear it, because a longer period gives the data more time to reach the capturing flip-flop.
Raising the supply voltage will clear it, because faster gates shrink the flip-flop's required hold time below the skew in the path.
Speeding up the data path will clear it, because new data must arrive well before the capturing clock edge.
Changing the clock period will not clear it; adding data-path delay is the usual fix, since hold is a same-edge race.

rubric: Hold compares data change against the same clock edge, so it is independent of period; the fix is more minimum data delay or less skew.
Distractors apply setup-time remedies (slower clock, faster path) to a hold problem.

items.prompt: A 4:1 multiplexer with selects S1 = A, S0 = B has data inputs I0 = C, I1 = 1, I2 = 0, I3 = C. It is meant to implement F = Σm(1,2,3,6,7) over A,B,C, with A as the MSB. For which input combination ABC is the output wrong?

options.label: ABC = 011
ABC = 111
ABC = 110
ABC = 001

rubric: For AB = 11 the intended data input is 1 (m6 and m7 are both in F), but the mux gives C, which is 0 for ABC = 110.
ABC = 111 gives C = 1, which is correct; the other choices fall in rows that are wired correctly.

items.prompt: A designer passes an asynchronous button signal through a two-flip-flop synchronizer into a synchronous FSM. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: The synchronizer guarantees the output can never be metastable, because both flip-flops share the same clock.
Passing a multi-bit count through one such synchronizer per bit is safe, because each bit settles on its own.
The output may lag the button by one or two clock cycles, so the FSM sees a delayed version of the signal.
The second flip-flop gives the first a full cycle to resolve, making a metastable value at its output very unlikely.

rubric: A two-flop synchronizer lowers the probability of metastability and adds up to two cycles of latency.
It never gives a guarantee, and per-bit synchronizing a bus can capture bits in different cycles, giving wrong values.

items.prompt: A student builds a Moore FSM that outputs 1 after the serial input has shown 101, overlap allowed. States: S0 (nothing useful), S1 (seen 1), S2 (seen 10), S3 (seen 101, output 1). On input 10101 it flags only the first 101 and misses the second. Which transition is the most likely fault?

options.label: From S3, input 0 goes to S0 instead of S2, losing the shared 1.
From S2, input 1 goes to S1 instead of S3, so the first 101 would never be flagged at all.
From S1, input 1 stays in S1 instead of returning to S0, so a run of 1s is treated as a fresh start.
From S3, input 1 goes to S0 instead of S1, so the new 1 after a match is ignored.

rubric: After 101 the suffix 10 is already a prefix of the next match, so S3 on 0 must go to S2; sending it to S0 loses the overlap.
Other options would break detection of the first 101 or describe transitions that are correct.

items.prompt: A 40-state controller targets an FPGA with abundant flip-flops. Criteria: maximise clock speed and keep state decoding simple; area is secondary. Which state encoding is best?

options.label: A minimised dense assignment from a tool, because it reduces next-state logic for all states and keeps the logic depth equal across all of them.
Binary, because 6 flip-flops give the fewest registers and therefore the shortest clock distribution path and the lowest clock skew.
One-hot, because each state is one bit, so decoding and next-state logic stay shallow despite needing 40 flip-flops.
Gray code, because only one bit changes per transition, which removes glitches and makes the decoding logic shallow for every state.

rubric: One-hot uses many flip-flops but gives shallow logic and fast clocks, matching the stated criteria.
Distractors optimise register count or transition bits, which are not the stated priorities.

items.prompt: A 32-bit adder must have a delay of at most about one third of a ripple-carry adder, while area may grow only modestly (not several times). Which design best fits?

options.label: Full Kogge-Stone parallel-prefix adder, because it has the lowest depth and its large area and wiring cost is acceptable.
Carry-save adder, because it removes carry propagation entirely and delivers the final sum in a single gate level.
Carry-lookahead adder from 4-bit groups with a second-level lookahead unit, giving far fewer carry stages for modest extra gates.
Ripple-carry adder with upsized gates, because it has the smallest area and its delay becomes acceptable once the gates are sized.

rubric: Grouped carry-lookahead shortens the carry path a lot for a modest area increase, meeting both criteria.
Ripple misses the delay target, Kogge-Stone breaks the area limit, and carry-save defers carries rather than producing a final sum.

items.prompt: A teammate divides a 100 MHz clock by 4 with a counter and wires its output to the clock pins of other flip-flops. Criteria: robust timing closure and easy analysis across blocks. Which critique is best?

options.label: Keep one 100 MHz clock and use a clock-enable pulse every fourth cycle; a derived clock adds skew and unintended clock-domain crossings.
It is acceptable as is, because a counter output is a clean synchronous signal that timing tools treat as the same clock.
Add a buffer to the divided clock, which aligns it exactly with the source clock and removes the need for crossing analysis.
Use a ripple divider instead, since it adds no combinational logic on the clock path and so removes all skew.

rubric: A single clock with enables keeps all flip-flops in one domain, which simplifies timing closure.
Distractors assume derived clocks are automatically aligned or that more clock-path logic removes skew.

items.prompt: A FIFO write pointer must be read in an unrelated clock domain. Criterion: the receiver must never see a value far from any true pointer value, even if sampling is mistimed. Which encoding is best?

options.label: Binary, because a two-flop synchronizer on each bit guarantees all bits are captured in the same cycle.
Binary sent twice in succession, because two matching copies prove that no bit was mid-transition at sampling.
Gray code, because only one bit changes per increment, so a mistimed sample is either the old or the new value.
Binary with a parity bit, because parity flags a bad sample and the reader can simply discard it and wait.

rubric: Gray code changes one bit per step, so any sampled value is at most one count off.
Binary variants can capture a mix of old and new bits; parity or repeated copies do not guarantee consistent capture.

items.prompt: Criteria: build Y = A XOR B using only 2-input NAND gates, with the fewest gates. Which implementation is best?

options.label: 4 gates: N1 = NAND(A,B); N2 = NAND(A,N1); N3 = NAND(B,N1); Y = NAND(N2,N3).
5 gates: NAND(A,A) and NAND(B,B) as inverters, NANDs for A·B' and A'·B, then a final NAND to OR them.
3 gates: N1 = NAND(A,B); N2 = NAND(N1,A); Y = NAND(N2,B).
6 gates: invert A and B, form A·B' and A'·B with NANDs, then NAND those and invert the result.

rubric: Sharing N1 gives a correct XOR with 4 NANDs, the known minimum.
The 3-gate circuit is not an XOR, and the 5- and 6-gate circuits are correct or nearly so but waste gates on inverters.

items.prompt: A controller drives an external device that samples its outputs at arbitrary times. Criteria: outputs must be glitch-free and change at predictable times after the clock; one extra cycle of latency is acceptable. Which choices fit? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add delay elements to the outputs, since they filter out every hazard without depending on the clock.
Register each output in a flip-flop, so hazards settle before the clock edge captures the value.
Use Moore outputs with extra output flip-flops, so output changes occur only shortly after clock edges.
Keep Mealy outputs combinational from the inputs, since they react a cycle sooner and settle fast enough in practice.

rubric: Registered outputs, including Moore outputs with output flip-flops, change only after a clock edge and cannot show combinational hazards.
Combinational Mealy outputs and delay elements leave hazards or unpredictable timing.

items.prompt: A decade counter wraps using a combinational decoder of the count that drives the flip-flops' asynchronous clear. It sometimes resets early or counts erratically because the decoder glitches as bits change. Criteria: fix with the least timing risk while keeping one clock. Which is best?

options.label: Halve the clock frequency, so the decoder has more time to settle before the clear acts.
Add redundant product terms in the decoder to remove every hazard, so the asynchronous clear only sees clean values.
Add a small RC delay on the clear line, so brief glitches are too short to reset the flip-flops.
Feed the decoded terminal count to the counter's synchronous clear or load input, so only the value at the clock edge matters.

rubric: A synchronous clear samples the decoder only at the clock edge, so glitches between edges are harmless.
The other fixes keep an asynchronous path that stays fragile: RC delays vary, hazard-free covers fail for multi-bit changes, and clock speed does not stop glitches.

items.prompt: F = AB + A'C is built as two-level AND-OR logic. With B=C=1, input A falls from 1 to 0, and F feeds an asynchronous latch that must not see a glitch. No clock is available and added logic must be minimal. Which fix is best?

options.label: Register F in a flip-flop so the latch sees changes only after an edge
Use a faster inverter on A so the A' term rises before the AB term falls
Add the redundant consensus term BC so F stays 1 while A changes
Reduce F to its minimal cover so that no redundant gates remain to glitch

rubric: The consensus term BC covers the transition, removing the static-1 hazard with one gate.
Faster inverters only shift timing without guaranteeing a fix, and minimal covers are the ones that have the hazard.

items.prompt: A controller output drives a peripheral that malfunctions on any glitch and may change only once per clock. The controller's inputs are noisy, unsynchronised switches. Judged against these criteria, which implementation is best?

options.label: Moore, with outputs taken directly from state flip-flops so noisy inputs cannot reach them
Mealy, because it needs fewer states and fewer gates, and therefore generates fewer glitches on its outputs
Mealy, because its output tracks the inputs within the same cycle and so reacts most precisely to changes
Either style, because both are synchronous machines and so their outputs can never glitch at all

rubric: Moore outputs from state registers change only at clock edges, isolating the output from input noise.
Mealy outputs are combinational functions of the inputs, so noise passes straight through.

items.prompt: Read and write pointers of an asynchronous FIFO cross between two unrelated clock domains. Which is the strongest justification for Gray-coding them?

options.label: Only one bit changes per increment, so a sampled pointer is either the old or new value, never a mixed one
Gray counters increment faster than binary because they have no carry chain, so the sampled pointer is always current
Gray counters need fewer flip-flops than binary, so there are fewer paths to synchronise across the two clock domains
Gray coding removes metastability from the sampled bits, so the synchroniser flops can be dropped from the crossing

rubric: Single-bit change means a mis-sampled pointer is off by at most one count, which is safe for full/empty logic.
Gray coding does not remove metastability or save flops; synchronisers are still required.

items.prompt: Post-layout timing shows a 0.3 ns hold violation between two flip-flops on the same clock, with positive setup slack. A colleague proposes lowering the clock frequency to fix it. Which judgement is best?

options.label: It works, because a longer period gives the data more time to settle before the capturing edge
It fails, because only raising the supply voltage speeds up the gates enough to remove hold violations
It works, because a slower clock reduces the skew between the two flops in proportion to the period
It fails, because hold is checked against the same edge and is independent of period; add delay on the data path

rubric: Hold compares data arrival with the same capturing edge, so period does not change it; delaying the data path does.
Distractors confuse hold with setup or propose changes that worsen it.

items.prompt: A 12-bit counter runs at a high clock rate, and its outputs are decoded to select memory banks, where any transient wrong count causes a bad access. Which counter style is best?

options.label: Ripple counter with a longer clock period, because the delay then settles within a cycle and has no effect
Ripple counter, because fewer gates and lower power outweigh transients that the decoders will mask
Synchronous counter, because all bits change on one edge and decoded outputs see only skew-sized transients
Synchronous counter, because it needs no carry logic and is therefore always smaller than a ripple design

rubric: In a synchronous counter all flops switch together, so invalid intermediate counts last only about the skew.
Ripple counters pass through invalid counts for accumulated delay; synchronous ones need extra carry logic.

items.prompt: A design asserts reset asynchronously, but a raw external button releases reset directly into 50 flip-flops across the chip. Which evaluations are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Flops leaving reset in different cycles can put a state machine into an illegal state
Asynchronous assertion is unsafe in all cases, so reset must be synchronous to be valid
Asynchronous reset needs no recovery or removal checks in timing analysis because it is not data
Release near a clock edge can violate recovery or removal timing, leaving some flops in reset and others out
A reset synchroniser that asserts asynchronously and releases synchronously keeps fast assertion and fixes release

rubric: Deassertion is effectively a timing-critical signal; synchronising release fixes it while retaining asynchronous assertion.
Recovery and removal checks are required, and asynchronous assertion alone is not the problem.

items.prompt: A team implements a 12-state controller in an FPGA with abundant flip-flops and 4-input LUTs. The binary-encoded version needs three LUT levels in its next-state logic and misses the clock target. Area is not a concern. Which encoding change best fits?

options.label: Keep minimum-length binary and treat unused codes as don't-cares, since that guarantees the shallowest logic
Switch to a compact 4-bit encoding hand-assigned to minimise bit changes, since fewer state bits always give faster logic
Switch to one-hot, since each next-state bit depends on few predecessors and depth shrinks at the cost of flops
Switch to Gray encoding, since single-bit transitions guarantee fewer LUT levels in every next-state function

rubric: One-hot trades flip-flops for shallow next-state and output logic, which suits timing-limited FPGA designs.
Gray or don't-care tweaks do not guarantee shallower logic.

items.prompt: Implement F = majority(A,B,C), which is 1 when at least two inputs are 1, using one 4:1 mux with A as the MSB select and B as the LSB select, plus at most one inverter. Which data inputs I0,I1,I2,I3 work?
rubric: With AB=00 the output is 0, with AB=01 or 10 it equals C, and with AB=11 it is 1.
Other options mis-assign the cofactors of the majority function.

items.prompt: Design a synchronous decade (0 to 9) counter from a 4-bit binary counter that has a synchronous clear. The outputs must never show 1010 even briefly, and no asynchronous clear is allowed. Which design meets this?

options.label: Detect Q=1111 and assert the synchronous clear, so the counter wraps after skipping the invalid codes
Detect Q=1010 and drive the asynchronous clear, so the count is reset immediately
Detect Q=1001 and assert the synchronous clear, so the next edge loads 0000 instead of 1010
Detect Q=1010 and assert the synchronous clear, so the following edge returns the count to 0000

rubric: Detecting 1001 means the next edge goes directly to 0000 and 1010 never appears.
Detecting 1010 lets the invalid code appear for a cycle or glitch, and 1111 is too late.

items.prompt: You must design a Moore-type, overlapping detector for the serial pattern 101, whose output is 1 only in the state reached after the last bit of a match. What is the minimum number of states?
rubric: States are: no progress, seen 1, seen 10, seen 101; overlap sends 101 on a 1 to 'seen 1' and on a 0 to 'seen 10'.
Three states would be the Mealy count, since a Moore output needs its own state.

items.prompt: A single-cycle event pulse from a 200 MHz domain must reach a 20 MHz domain without ever being lost, even though the pulse is only one source cycle wide. Which design meets this?

options.label: AND the pulse with the destination clock so that the slow domain captures it only on a clock edge
Send the pulse straight through a two-flop synchroniser in the destination domain, which resolves metastability and keeps the pulse
Stretch the pulse to two source cycles and then synchronise it, which makes the pulse wide enough to be sampled
Toggle a source flop on each event, synchronise it with two flops in the destination, and XOR successive samples to regenerate the pulse

rubric: A toggle is a level change that persists until sampled, so a short pulse cannot be missed, and XOR recovers the event.
Direct synchronisation or short stretching can miss a 5 ns pulse in a 50 ns sampling period; ANDing with a clock is glitch-prone.

items.prompt: In a 4-bit adder, c2 must be produced in two gate levels directly from c0 and the per-bit signals g_i = A_i B_i and p_i = A_i XOR B_i, without waiting for c1. Which expression should the design use?

options.label: c2 = g1 + g0 + p1 p0 c0, combining all generate terms directly
c2 = g1 + p1 g0 + p1 p0 c0, expanding c1 in terms of g0, p0 and c0
c2 = g1 + p1 c1, taking the previous carry from the first stage
c2 = g1 p1 + g0 p0 c0, ANDing each generate with its own propagate

rubric: Substituting c1 = g0 + p0 c0 into c2 = g1 + p1 c1 gives the flat lookahead form.
The other options either ripple through c1 or are not the carry function.

items.prompt: A 6-state traffic controller uses a 3-bit binary encoding, leaving 2 codes unused. It must recover from any illegal state within one cycle and not hang after power-up or noisy asynchronous inputs. Which additions meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Replace the flip-flops with level-sensitive latches so state settles faster after noise
Define next-state entries for the unused codes that return to the idle state
Provide a power-on reset that forces the machine into a known state
Pass asynchronous inputs through two-flop synchronisers before they reach the next-state logic
Treat unused codes as don't-cares so the minimiser makes the logic cheaper, since they never occur

rubric: Explicit recovery transitions, a known start state and synchronised inputs prevent hangs and metastability-driven illegal states.
Don't-cares leave recovery undefined, and latches add timing hazards.

items.prompt: A push-button feeds a design clocked at 1 MHz. Contact bounce lasts up to 5 ms, the button is asynchronous to the clock, and each press must produce exactly one one-clock pulse with release bounce also ignored. Which design satisfies all of this?

options.label: Two-flop synchroniser, then a counter that accepts a new level after it persists over 5000 cycles, then a rising-edge detect
Edge detection on the raw button input, followed by a 5 ms timer that blocks later edges and ignores release bounce
Slowing the system clock to 100 Hz so that bounces fall between samples, and using no further logic at all
A synchroniser followed by a rising-edge detect and a 50-cycle lockout, since the bounce is far shorter than a millisecond

rubric: Synchronise, require a stable level for longer than the bounce (5000 cycles at 1 MHz), then detect the clean edge.
Short lockouts miss the 5 ms bounce, raw-input edge detection is unsynchronised, and slowing the clock does not guarantee clean sampling.
